A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REFDIV study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

before.justification: v1 reports original AdvBench attack experiments, entropy analyses, transferability evaluations, and reward-model and sampling-budget experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, model evaluations, mitigation tests, sensitivity studies, and quantitative entropy analyses.

M1.justification: The default genetic algorithm, fitness objective, and exponential weighting schedule remain unchanged. Appendix G.2 adds tested linear and sigmoid weighting variants, providing limited adaptations of the optimization procedure. Newly documented genetic operators and MCTS steps do not establish other method changes.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 520-query AdvBench dataset for adversarial safety and transferability tasks. Additional target models, filtering procedures, and sensitivity settings expand experimental configurations without introducing another dataset, domain, or task.

E2.justification: AutoDAN-Turbo changes from cited related work to an evaluated third attack baseline throughout Table 1 and Figures 2–3. Figure 4 also expands the entropy comparison from AutoDAN versus REFDIV to include GCG and AutoDAN-Turbo, substantially broadening the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 adds four open-source target models and Claude-3.5-Haiku, ToxiGuardRail reward-model evaluations, a two-child/two-iteration MCTS configuration, alternative weighting schedules, and pooled perplexity filtering at 10% and 20% using Qwen2.5-7B. These are additional experimental settings; the original generation settings and main evaluation configurations are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses examine perplexity-filter resistance, MCTS-budget and weighting-schedule sensitivity, linguistic explanations for transferability, and entropy reduction and its association with ASR. Appendix C additionally tests ToxiGuardRail. The existing sampling-budget, MCTS-entropy, and DeBERTa analyses remain, although some are newly framed as mitigation tests.

E5.justification: Appendix H introduces Pearson correlation estimation between entropy and ASR, reported in Table 10. Neither version specifies seeds, repeated-run counts, or confidence intervals. Shaded plot bands already appear in v1, so their presence in v2 does not establish newly introduced uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 ASRs, Table 2 values, and existing Table 3 rows are retained. Substantial new results include AutoDAN-Turbo comparisons, Claude transferability, mitigation and sensitivity outcomes, and entropy statistics. For example, new Table 4 reports REFDIV/AutoDAN ASRs of 0.943/0.858 on Llama3.1-70B; these are additional-model results, not improvements over v1 under the same setting.

T1.justification: Appendix G.2 newly defines the sigmoid and linear weighting functions used in sensitivity experiments. The original LLM/TTS formalism, ASR definition, entropy measures, and fitness objective remain mathematically equivalent; the revised notation in Equation 1 is cosmetic. No theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The central claim that suppressing candidate diversity exposes a transferable TTS safety failure remains. The final introductory contribution broadens from bypassing guardrail classifiers to resisting several mitigation strategies, and the closed-source transfer claim explicitly includes Claude-3.5-Haiku.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning weighting-schedule insensitivity, modest entropy reductions, linguistic mechanisms behind transferability, and possible AutoDAN-Turbo skill-library mismatch. It reframes existing sampling-budget results as evidence against increasing candidate counts as a defense and explicitly acknowledges that safety-specific verifiers can reduce ASR without eliminating attacks.

D1.justification: Appendix E newly documents crossover and mutation rates, mutation operations, and MCTS expansion, selection, judging, backpropagation, and final selection. Appendix I supplies reward-model provenance and specifications. Most original implementation settings move from Appendix D to J unchanged, while the direct AutoDAN codebase link is omitted.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references for perplexity defenses, curriculum learning, MCTS implementations, reward models, and additional evaluated models, while removing generic LLM-application citations from the introduction. The overall diversity-based research positioning remains, with an added practical contrast against AutoDAN-Turbo. AutoDAN-Turbo itself was already cited in v1.

P1.justification: The introduction and related work are tightened, transferability headings emphasize black-box access, and Section 4.6 becomes a mitigation section with four subsections. An impact statement is added and the original implementation appendix moves to J. The main section sequence and much of the methodological explanation remain intact.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from predominantly single-column formatting to two columns, with widespread figure relocation and restyling of plot colors, markers, axes, and typography. Table 1 gains a baseline column, Figure 6 gains Claude results, Table 3 expands, and Tables 4–10 are added. The original method schematic is retained.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses gaps in v1's comparator coverage, MCTS and weighting-schedule sensitivity checks, and implementation documentation, improving empirical scrutiny and reproducibility. The gain is limited by reporting weaknesses: Table 7 gives ASRs of 0.846/0.963 for the nominal three-child/three-iteration MCTS configuration, versus 0.831/0.967 in Table 1, without reconciliation. Run-count and uncertainty documentation remain inadequate, and the added correlation analysis does not establish the claimed causal mechanism.
